solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Nick, the party attack dog?

definitions.note: One half is a noun and the other a verb, which is normal in a double definition: the answer has both lives, and only one of them can be read at a time.

blocks.note: to nick something is to steal it, and this is the slang verb for making off with a thing
the MP whose job is to drive colleagues through the voting lobbies and savage the ones who stray

explanation.surface: A man called Nick cast as his party's snarling enforcer.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick opens with a capital and looks like a name, and the comma after it is doing the work of an equals sign. A party whip in Westminster enforces discipline, so the question mark owns up to 'attack dog' as a job description.
explanation.definitionFit: A whip is the MP who bullies colleagues into voting the right way, and to whip something is to nick it.

clue.text: Bloody hell! Law enforcement leaders harass the speaker

indicators.note: whoever leads is out in front of the rest, so each of the two words hands over only the letter it starts with

blocks.note: the polite four-letter stand-in people say when they are swearing but not quite
the opening letters of the two-word phrase, in the order written

explanation.surface: An outraged oath about police chiefs hounding whoever is addressing the room.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital-S Speaker of the Commons lurks behind the surface, and the definition wants the ordinary sense — anyone holding the floor. Barracking a candidate at a rally is the picture the answer belongs to.
explanation.definitionFit: To heckle is to shout a speaker down while they are speaking, which is harassment aimed at whoever has the floor.

clue.text: Do row, as subdued MPs stand by

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer by what loyal MPs do with it rather than offering a noun that swaps straight in — it is the thing they keep to, not a synonym.

blocks.note: a do is a knees-up, the British word for any celebration with drink at it
a row of seats or houses is a line of them

explanation.surface: Have the argument, while cowed backbenchers look on and do nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand by' looks like standing idly while a row goes on, and the definition needs the other sense — standing by something out of loyalty. In Westminster the whipped-in position is what a rebel breaks and a loyalist repeats.
explanation.definitionFit: The party line is the agreed position a party's MPs are expected to vote for and defend in public.

clue.text: (& 7ac.) Become snotty-nosed and collar Conservative veteran

blocks.note: to collar a suspect is to grab hold of him and take him into custody
C is the single letter beside a candidate's name on a British ballot paper
a veteran of anything has been at it a long time

explanation.surface: Coming down with a streaming nose while grabbing an elderly Tory by the collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snotty-nosed' means stuck-up as well as streaming, and the sneering sense is what the surface wants. The answer runs on into 7 across, so the five letters in this light are only the first half of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch cold is to come down with one, and a running nose is the symptom anybody names first.

clue.text: (&19dn.) Votes cast by Burnham's top information expert for the 'Refuse' candidate?

indicators.note: the top of a name is the letter it starts with, and in a down entry that is the letter nearest the top of the grid

blocks.note: the tally of ballots on election night is the sense of 'votes cast' here
the opening letter of the name of Andy Burnham, the Mayor of Greater Manchester
inf. is the dictionary's clipped form of the word
an ace at something is the person who does it better than anyone

explanation.surface: A data specialist from Andy Burnham's office totting up ballots for the anti-rubbish candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: Count Binface is the joke candidate who stands at British elections wearing a bin lid and a cape, so 'Refuse' is both the rubbish he campaigns about and the rejection a protest vote makes. His title is a pun on counting votes.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation marks around Refuse point at both senses at once — the bin the candidate wears and the vote that turns everyone else down.

clue.text: Mark Dicky's carpet

blocks.note: the small mark a teacher puts beside a right answer
feeling dicky is British for feeling off, as in a dicky heart

explanation.surface: Noting something down on Richard's floor covering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' is the verb: to be carpeted is to be called in for a dressing-down, from being made to stand on the boss's rug. Mark reads as a second man's name beside Dicky and is an instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To tick someone off is to give them a telling-off, which is exactly what carpeting a person means.

clue.text: "Hard in the morning" fellow lives with Edward – awkward

indicators.note: a thing that is in something sits inside it, so the letter named before it drops between the two letters of the piece named after

blocks.note: H is stamped on a pencil for hard, and is the crossword's usual single letter for it
ante meridiem, the two letters on any clock before noon
F for fellow is the letter in the strings after an academic's name, as in FRS
a man who lives is a man who is, in the third person as written
Ted is the everyday short form of the name

explanation.surface: A man boasting about his mornings, sharing a house with Edward, to everybody's embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks fence off the boast so it reads as speech rather than as two instructions. Clumsy hands are the picture behind the answer — a fist where fingers should be — and nothing in the surface points at them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ham-fisted handles things as though wearing boxing gloves, which is what calling a person awkward or clumsy says.

clue.text: see 4ac.
Clearing organ out? Hang on

indicators.note: to take something out is to remove it, so the letters named leave the word they were sitting in

blocks.note: the eight-letter word to be trimmed, taken as it stands
the ear is the organ of hearing, and its three letters sit together in the middle of the longer word

explanation.surface: Someone clearing an organ out and being told to wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clearing' does double duty: it is the word to be cut and it makes the surface sound medical. 'Hang on' is the physical sense, gripping something, not the telephone one.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling to a ledge or a parent is to hang on and not let go, so the verbs swap straight over.

clue.text: Ability to read French article about sex – risqué!

indicators.note: to be about something is to be round it, so the two letters just clued close over what follows

blocks.note: le is the masculine 'the' in French, the grammarian's article rather than a magazine piece
'it' is the coy old word for sex and sex appeal, as in the It girl
a racy story is a slightly indecent one

explanation.surface: A French piece about sex that turns out to be near the knuckle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammar word — a, an, the — and its French form is where crosswords get two letters at a stroke. The It girl was Clara Bow in the 1920s, and the usage stuck.
explanation.definitionFit: Literacy is the ability to read and write, so the noun stands in for the phrase without any stretching.

clue.text: Holiday spot in which – phwoar! – female undoes top

indicators.note: the top of a word is the letter it begins with, and only that one letter is wanted

blocks.note: the British noise of appreciation that phwoar spells out at greater length
F is the standard single letter for female, from forms and passports
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A resort where an appreciative cry goes up as a woman takes her top off.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes fence the leer off so the rest still reads as a travel note. 'Top' is the garment on the surface and the first letter of a word in the wordplay — the same trick Cyclops uses at 4 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is the Ionian island that British package tours have flown to for decades, so the definition names the class and the answer is one member of it.

clue.text: Be left to have an orgasm? Not I, sadly

indicators.note: letters in a sorry state are letters out of order, and the word invites you to take them badly

blocks.note: the blunt verb for it, which the question mark flags as slang
these four letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: Being abandoned so someone can finish alone, which the speaker regrets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be left' is the money sense — what a will leaves you, you come into — and nothing in the surface points at inheritance. 'Not I' is the sort of two-word protest that reads as speech and turns out to be fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into a fortune is to inherit it, which is what being left something in somebody's will amounts to.

clue.text: Wife leaves twerp for associate

indicators.note: when someone leaves they are no longer there, so that letter goes missing from the word it was in

blocks.note: a wally is a British idiot, an insult that peaked in the 1980s and never quite went
W for wife is the abbreviation from family trees, and it is the letter that departs

explanation.surface: A wife walking out on an idiot and taking up with a colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as the wife's departure and instructs a deletion, which is why the sentence sounds like gossip rather than an instruction. The letter she takes with her is the one she stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is someone on your side in a common cause, so 'associate' matches it as a noun for a partner rather than an enemy.

clue.text: Whisky drink raised in vulgar defiance?

definitions.note: Neither half is a synonym: one measures a drink by the depth it fills a glass, the other describes a gesture, and both land on the same noun phrase.

blocks.note: spirits are poured by the finger, the depth in the glass judged against the hand holding it
the British insult made with the hand, palm inwards, that says what the person will not say aloud

explanation.surface: A large Scotch lifted in a rude toast.
explanation.walkthrough: The British version of the gesture turns the palm inwards, which is what separates it from the American one finger and from Churchill's V for victory. The question mark owns up to the joke of measuring both in fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Two fingers is both the barman's measure of whisky and the name of the palm-inwards insult, which is how one phrase answers both halves.

clue.text: Family party, fine to some extent

blocks.note: your kin are your relatives, the word that survives in next of kin
a do is a party, the British word for the event itself
F is the grade stamped on a pencil for a fine point

explanation.surface: A family knees-up that turned out passably well.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short words in a row each hand over their crossword value, and the seam between wordplay and definition falls after 'fine' with no link word to mark it. 'Kind of' is the hedge that shades whatever follows it downwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Kind of tired means tired to some extent, so the two phrases do the same softening job in front of an adjective.

clue.text: Democrat with papers at bar – lacking vision?

blocks.note: D is the letter beside a Democrat's name on an American ballot
a ream is five hundred sheets, the crossword's standard supply of paper
bar in the sense of bar none means except, and so does less

explanation.surface: An American politician propping up the bar with his paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is the preposition of bar none — everything except — and not the counter the surface leans on. 'Vision' has to be the night-time kind rather than the ambition a politician is accused of lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamless sleep has no visions in it, so the adjective and the phrase both describe a night that passed with nothing seen.

clue.text: Subjects to tabloid photos?

indicators.note: a tabloid clips every word it can fit into a headline, so the long word gives way to the newsroom's short one

blocks.note: the little word is taken exactly as it stands in the clue
pics is what a red-top calls its pictures

explanation.surface: People being made the subject of a newspaper's picture spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subjects to' reads as one verb phrase — subjecting somebody to something — and that is the false path: the 'to' is a piece of the answer, and the definition is the first word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Topics are the subjects a conversation or an essay is about, and both words are plural nouns for the same thing.

clue.text: Grand old man, a rich prat's fancy

indicators.note: to fancy something up is to dress it out of its plain shape, and letters dressed up do not stay in the order given

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Some wealthy fool's idea of how he ought to be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand old man' is the set English phrase for an elder statesman, and the insult that supplies the letters is aimed at the same figure. The possessive 's is doing the work of 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriarch is the senior man a family, tribe or church defers to, which is the standing 'grand old man' describes.

clue.text: Situation requires a bit of opera or I shift

indicators.note: to shift something is to move it out of its place, and letters moved out of place come back in a different order

blocks.note: a scena is a scene in an opera, and the word is in the dictionary for exactly that
these three letters, moved about

explanation.surface: Someone insisting the situation calls for an operatic scene, or else they are off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scena' is worth banking: setters reach for it whenever 'a bit of opera' turns up, and it is not the first letter it looks like. 'Shift' passes as a threat to move house and is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A scenario is an outline of how things might stand — the situation a planner or a screenwriter sets out in advance.

clue.text: Cyclops pursuing school online far right conspiracy

indicators.note: to pursue someone is to come along behind them, so this piece is written after the ones it chases
in an across entry the far right is where the answer ends, which is where the chaser comes to rest

blocks.note: sch. is the standard abbreviation on a map or a school timetable
the e- of email and e-commerce is the prefix for anything done online
Cyclops is the name printed above this puzzle, so the setter naming himself means himself

explanation.surface: The setter trailing a school's internet activity into a far-right plot.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter who names himself in his own clue means 'me', and Cyclops has signed Private Eye's crossword since the 1970s. The far right is politics in the surface and the end of the row in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a plan laid in secret for someone else's cost, and a conspiracy is the same plan with more than one person in on it.

clue.text: Personal cleansers supplied by – wait – disheartened Trump supporters

indicators.note: to dishearten a phrase is to cut its heart out, leaving only the letters standing at either end

blocks.note: to bide is to wait, the verb that survives in biding your time
everything between the first letter of one word and the last of the other is thrown away

explanation.surface: Demoralised Trump fans handing out the bathroom fittings.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes fence 'wait' off as an aside, hiding that it is a word to translate rather than an interruption. A bidet is the low basin beside a French lavatory, which is the joke inside the prim definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bidets are the low bathroom basins made for washing your nether regions, so 'personal cleansers' is a polite plural way of naming them.

clue.text: see 4dn.
Church is into kinky sex, causing split

indicators.note: what goes into something ends up inside it, so the letters named first are planted in the middle of the ones named last

blocks.note: S&M is the shorthand for the rougher sort, and the crossword borrows it without its ampersand
ch. is the abbreviation printed beside a church on an Ordnance Survey map
the word is taken exactly as it stands

explanation.surface: A church caught up in kinky sex and tearing itself in two.
explanation.walkthrough: The Church of England arguing itself apart over sex is real enough to make the surface read like a headline, which is what hides the two-letter pieces. 'Is' being lifted whole is the hardest bit to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A schism is the formal split of a church or a party into rival camps, the noun for the moment one body becomes two.

clue.text: Put too little effort into digging for copper etc, being weakened

blocks.note: the prefix that turns any effort into not enough of it: underfunded, underplayed, undercooked
digging ore out of the ground is mining, and the past tense comes with it

explanation.surface: Slacking down the copper mine and losing your strength for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' points at the policeman first — the crossword's favourite trap — and here it is the metal being dug for. Mining under a wall is where the figurative sense of the answer comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To undermine something is to weaken it by digging away at what holds it up, so 'weakened' is the state it is left in.

clue.text: Mutt, blowing top, is symbolic of USA

definitions.note: The definition says what the answer stands for rather than offering a noun to swap in, which is the usual way of clueing a national emblem.

indicators.note: to blow something off is to send it flying, so the letter named next departs from the word it began

blocks.note: a beagle is a small hound, and any dog will do for a mutt
the top of a down word is the letter at its head, and that is the one lost

explanation.surface: A mongrel losing its temper, next to the emblem of America.
explanation.walkthrough: Blowing your top is losing your temper and also losing your first letter, one phrase doing both jobs. The bald eagle has carried the Great Seal of the United States since 1782.
explanation.definitionFit: The bald eagle is the bird on America's Great Seal, so it stands for the country on coins, passports and presidential lecterns.

clue.text: Bedding Victor to fill a twosome?

definitions.note: 'Bedding' here is the mass noun for what goes on a bed, not the verb the surface is leering at, so it names a thing rather than an action.

indicators.note: to fill something is to get inside it and take up the room, so the single letter drops into the middle of the other word

blocks.note: two singers performing together make a duet
Victor is V in the phonetic alphabet pilots and police use

explanation.surface: Taking a champion to bed to make up a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bedding' leers as a verb and turns out to be the quilt. Victor is the same alphabet that gives Whisky at 12 across, and it is always worth checking a proper name for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A duvet is the thick quilt that replaced sheets and blankets on British beds, so it sits squarely inside bedding.

clue.text: Yen's in shit? Cheers!

indicators.note: what is in something is contained by it, so the letters sit unbroken inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run on across the word break and the question mark, in the order written

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the currency is in trouble, then raising a glass anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' is the craving, not the Japanese currency the surface wants. Punctuation is no barrier to a hidden word — the question mark in the middle of the span is there to stop the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A yen for something is a nagging want, and an itch is that same craving felt as something you cannot leave alone.

clue.text: Heard dog's drunk Irish port

indicators.note: a drunk cannot walk a straight line, and these letters cannot keep to the line they were given

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A drunken dog overheard somewhere on the Irish quayside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' looks like a signal for a sound-alike and is fodder instead; the instruction is 'drunk'. Drogheda is the port on the River Boyne, thirty miles up the coast from Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: Drogheda stands at the mouth of the Boyne in County Louth and has worked as a port for centuries, so the definition names it by country and trade.

clue.text: He scored, lover did – well, not altogether

definitions.note: The definition is a clause about the man rather than a noun that swaps in, which is how a proper name with no synonym gets defined.

indicators.note: taking not all of something means taking only part of it, so a run inside the words is wanted rather than the words themselves

blocks.note: the letters run straight on from the end of one word into the next, and only the outer ends of the span are spare
the hesitation is surface only and carries no letters

explanation.surface: Gossip about how a lover performed, taken back halfway through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He scored' is the leer the surface wants and the composer's day job at the same time. Giuseppe Verdi wrote Rigoletto, La traviata and Aida, and a score is what an opera is written on.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi spent fifty years writing operatic scores, so 'he scored' names the man by the work rather than by any synonym.

clue.text: (& 28/29) House doubly full of humbug? There's nothing like it

definitions.note: The definition gives what the phrase means when somebody says it rather than a noun to swap in — the whole saying is a claim that nowhere else compares.

indicators.note: doubly means twice over, so the word it follows is written out a second time
something full of a thing has that thing inside it, so the doubled word opens up to take what comes next

blocks.note: the four-letter word for a house, written twice over
a humbug is a hard mint-striped boiled thing from a paper bag

explanation.surface: A house stuffed with mints, or with cant, depending which humbug is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: Humbug is both the boiled sweet and the nonsense a politician talks, and the question mark flags the pun. The answer is the sampler stitched on a Victorian wall, which is why the definition is a sentiment rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The old sampler motto says nowhere beats your own house, so 'there's nothing like it' is what a person means by saying it.
